statements.claim: Narada, standing in Dwaraka before his departure, recites Krishna's deeds one by one as if taking dictation.
statements.evidence: Pack index: 'Narada Prophesies the Ocean Will Swallow Dwarka || Before departing, Narada prophesies...' and Harivamsha 1.249 is Narada's recital of the same deeds.

statements.claim: The nooses made by Mura were cut; Nisumva and Naraka slain; the road to Pragyotish freed from dangers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249 (Dutt): 'the nooses made by Mura have been cut, Nisumva and Naraka have been slain and the road to the city of Pragyotish has been freed from all dangers.'

statements.claim: The kings of the world were frightened by the twang of Krishna's bow and the sound of the conch Panchajanya.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'the proud kings of the world have been frightened in battle by this descendant of Shura... with the twang of his bow and the sound of his conch-shell Panchajanya.'

statements.claim: Rukmi, protected by his Deccan chariot-warriors, was vanquished and Rukmini carried away in a car blazing like the sun and rumbling like a cloud.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having vanquished easily the highly powerful Rukshmi well protected by the Decean car-warriors resembling clouds... carried away Rukshmini... in a car effulgent like the sun and producing a rattle like unto the muttering of clouds.'

statements.claim: In Jaruthi, Ahdriti, Kratha and Shishupala fell; Dantavakra and Shatadhanwa with all their soldiers; Shalwa of the city Shoubha struck down; Dyumutsena struck by the discus.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'In the city of Jāruthi he defeated Ahdriti, Kratha and Shishupala and vanquished Dantavakra and Shatadhanwā with all their soldiers... the beautiful lord of Shoubha killed Shālwa... struck Dyumutsena with his discus.' The 'dashed from the sky' phrasing is atmospheric colour over the discus stroke.

statements.claim: Gopati and Talaketu, followers of Ravana on the summit of Mahendra, were killed in a twinkling; Hansa and Dimvaka slain after them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'In the city of Irāvati on the summit of the mount Mahendra there lived two followers of Rāvana Gopati and Tālaketu... killed them both, within the twinkling of an eye, the Dānavas Hansa and Dimvaka have been also slain by Krishna with their followers.'

statements.claim: Varanasi was burnt down; Maya killed with knotty arrows; the son of Indrasena released.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Vārānashi (Benares) has been burnt down by the high souled Keshava... Having killed Maya in battle with knotty arrows Krishna... has released the son of Indrasena.'

statements.claim: Varuna was defeated beneath the sea at Lohitakuta; the Parijata tree was carried off from Indra's palace though the celestials could not prevent it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'The highly powerful Varuna... has been defeated in battle by Krishna repairing to Lohitakuta (under water)'; 'Having gone to Indra's palace, he, although prevented by the highly powerful celestials, disregarding their king, carried away the Pārijāta tree.' Minor nuance: the pack has the celestials actively trying to prevent the taking, not passively 'forbidden to interfere' as the story phrases it; outcome is unchanged.

statements.claim: The kings of Pandya, Poundrya, Kalinga, Matsa and Banga were slain; Kaliya was despatched from the river to the sea; Yama was vanquished and restored the dead son of Sandipani.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'The intelligent Janārddana has slain the kings of Pandya, Poundrya, Kalinga, Matsa and Banga'; 'defeated in water the highly powerful Nāga king Kālya... despatched him to the sea'; 'Having vanquished Vivaswān's son Yama, Hari... has restored to life the dead son of Sāndipani.'

statements.claim: In his dwarf form Krishna took the three worlds from Bali; Kamsa's courtiers Peetha, Paithika and Asitoma were killed; the Daityas Jambha, Airavata and Virupa were slain while he wore the semblance of a man.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'in his pristine dwarfish form Mādhava stole away from Bali the three worlds'; 'killed Peetha, Paithika and Asitomā the courtiers of the long-armed Kansa'; 'killed the Daityas Jambha, Airāvata and Virupa, assuming the semblance of a man.'

statements.claim: Arjuna was crowned with success and Drona, Bhishma, Karna and Suyodhana were defeated; the daughter of the king of Suveera was carried away to please Vabhru.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'the Lord Madhusudana has crowned the foremost of Bharatas, Arjuna... with success'; 'defeated, in battle, Drona, Drauni, Karna, Bhishma, Suyodhana and other warriors'; 'For pleasing Vabhru the powerful Hari... carried away by force the daughter of the king of Suveera.' Naming the field 'Kurukshetra' is contextual gloss beyond the chapter text but consistent with the war described.

statements.claim: Having established virtue among mortals through sacrifices and accomplished the work of the gods, Krishna would return to his own region, and the ocean would devour Bhogavati and Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having established virtue amongst the mortals by performing various sacrifices and accomplished the great work of the gods he will return to his own region. Then the highly illustrious Krishna will make the ocean devour the cities Bhogavati, a favourite resort of the Rishis, and Dwārakā.'

statements.claim: The city of jewels and sacrificial grounds would sink with its gardens into Varuna's abode; none among gods, Asuras or men except the slayer of Madhu would be able to live there.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'This city of Dwārakā, filled with various jewels and sacrificial grounds, will enter, with its gardens, into the abode (sea) of Varuna... constructed by Vāsudeva and resembling the residence of the sun. There is none amongst the gods, Asuras, and men and none will be, except the slayer of Madhu, who will be able to live here.'

statements.claim: Having instituted his regulations among the Dasharhas, Vishnu would be united with Narayana, Soma and Surya.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having thus instituted many excellent regulations amongst the Dāshārhas Vishnu himself will be united with Nārāyana, Shoma and Surya.' ('As fire returns to fire' is figurative imagery.)

statements.claim: Krishna heard the prophecy without arguing, and Narada took his leave while Dwaraka continued its day above the waiting sea.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting around the recital/prophecy; matches the pack's 'before departing' frame. Krishna's silent reception and the waiting-sea imagery are atmosphere, not pack-asserted facts.

notes: Close, largely verbatim rendering of the Harivamsha 1.249 recital; every named deed, list and prophecy detail maps to the passage. Two micro-nuances only: 'forbidden to interfere' (pack says the celestials tried to prevent the Parijata removal but were disregarded) and 'at Kurukshetra' as a locational gloss not named in the chapter. Neither rises to UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: The Yadu boys, giddy and reckless, dressed Samba, son of Jambavati, in women's clothes and led him to the visiting sages claiming the veiled boy was pregnant.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.13-15 and VP 5.37: boys disguised 'Samba, the son of Jambavatī, as a woman' (BP 11.1.13: sāmbaṃ jāmbavatī-sutam); VP (Wilson): 'they dressed and adorned Sumba, the son of Jámbavatí, as a damsel.' Pack excerpt: boys asked 'This dark-eyed one is pregnant; what will she give birth to?'

statements.claim: The sages, undeceived, answered in anger that 'she' would bear an iron mace that would destroy the clan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.15 (kupitā: angered): pack excerpt 'The angry sages answered: She will bear an iron mace, the destroyer of your clan.' VP 5.37: 'She will bring forth a club, that shall crush the whole of the Yádava race.'

statements.claim: The mace came forth from Samba's belly on the spot, and the terrified boys cried 'What have we done, ill-fated as we are? What will people say of us now?'
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.16-17: 'te 'ti-santrastā vimucya sahasodaram / kiṃ kṛtaṃ manda-bhāgyair naḥ kiṃ vadiṣyanti no janāḥ' — terrified, they released it from the belly and lamented exactly that. VP 5.37 confirms a club 'was produced from the belly of Śámba.'

statements.claim: The boys carried the mace to the assembly; Ugrasena, the Yadava king, had it ground to powder and the powder cast into the sea.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.18-20: 'tac copanīya sadasi... yadu-rājaḥ sa āhukaḥ' — carried it to the assembly; Ahuka (Ugrasena) the Yadu king ground the mace to powder and had it thrown into the water. VP 5.37: Ugrasena had the iron club ground to dust and thrown into the sea.

statements.claim: A fish swallowed a scrap of the iron among the powder in the sea; the fish was caught by fishermen, and the iron was eventually worked into the arrow that waited in a hunter's quiver.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.21-22: 'kaścin matsyo 'grasīl lohaṃ cūrṇāṇi taralaiḥ tataḥ / matsyo gṛhīto matsya-ghnair jālenānyaiḥ sahārṇave' — a fish swallowed the iron with the powder in the waters and was caught by fishermen with nets. Pack index excerpt: the last bit of iron 'in the hunter's hands became the arrow.' (The working through later hands is the standard BP continuation of the same episode; pack summary supports the fish-to-arrow chain.)

statements.claim: Krishna was not surprised when the news reached him: the sages had pronounced the curse knowing the mind of the Lord, and holy anger was an instrument of a design already made.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.23: the sages, angered by the Yadu and Bhoja boys at play, cursed them 'knowing the mind of the Lord' (bhagavan-mata-kovidāḥ). MB 16.1 excerpt (in pack): 'The slayer of Madhu, informed of what had taken place, summoned all the Vrishnis...' — Krishna is informed and does not overturn the sentence.

statements.claim: He gathered the Vrishnis to him so that when the curse ripened they would be found together; the clan kept its city while the curse settled over the house.
statements.evidence: Krishna's summoning of the Vrishnis is in the pack (MB 16.1 excerpt); the motive gloss ('so that when it arrives, they will be found together') and the closing 'curse settled over the house' imagery are the story's interpretive framing, not pack statements.

notes: Faithful composite of BP 11.1.13-23 (joke, curse, mace birth, lament, assembly, grinding, fish) with VP 5.37 (Samba as Jambavati's son) and BP 3.3.23 (sages knowing the Lord's mind). All characters, sequence and outcome match the pack; no UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Uddhava recalls Krishna's deliberation after the great war: with Drona, Bhishma, Arjuna and Bhima gone, the remaining burden of the earth was the unbearable host of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13: 'kiyān bhuvo 'yaṃ kṣapitoru-bhāro yad droṇa-bhīṣmārjuna-bhīma-mūlaiḥ' — what burden of earth remained when Drona, Bhishma, Arjuna and Bhima (its roots) were gone; pack excerpt: 'the unbearable host of the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: The Yadava host numbered eighteen akshauhinis and could be destroyed by no enemy.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13 (Sanskrit): 'aṣṭādaśākṣauhiṇiko mad-aṃśair āste balaṃ durviṣahaṃ yadūnām' — the invincible Yadava army of eighteen akshauhinis. Pack summary: 'could be destroyed in no other way than by their own quarrel.'

statements.claim: Krishna's words: 'When they quarrel among themselves, eyes red with wine, there is no other way to destroy them' and 'When I act, they will vanish of themselves.'
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.14: 'mitho yadaiṣāṃ bhavitā vivādo madhv-āmadātāmra-vilocanānām / naiṣāṃ vadhopāya iyān ato 'nyo mayy udyate 'ntardadhate svayaṃ sma' — matches the pack's rendered excerpt verbatim in substance.

statements.claim: The destruction would come through their own quarrel under the pretext of the brahmins' curse on Samba — the iron mace — which Krishna recognised as the door.
statements.evidence: Pack variant note cross-refs vp5_037_03 (extermination of the Yadava race 'by the pretext of an imprecation denounced by Brahmans' — the Samba/iron-mace episode, VP 5.37); BP 3.3's own continuation (v.23, in the corpus chain) has the sages curse the boys. The curse-as-pretext reading is the pack's canonical event (evt_0285, recall of the self-destruction).

statements.claim: No war could be fought against the Yadavas and won; the only way to lighten the earth of them was to let them destroy themselves, wine in their eyes, at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13-14 and pack summary ('the Yadu warriors... could be destroyed in no other way than by their own quarrel, and that when he acted, they would destroy themselves'); the festive ride to Prabhasa is the follow-on in the same Uddhava recollection (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain.

statements.claim: Staging: Krishna spoke these words aloud to Uddhava in Dwaraka, and Uddhava remembered them for the rest of his life.
statements.evidence: The pack presents the deliberation as Uddhava's recollection of Krishna's reflection (uddhava uvāca; 'evam sañcintya bhagavān...'); rendering it as a direct conversation is a dramatisation of that recall, faithful in content.

notes: Substantive claims (burden analysis, 18 akshauhinis, wine-reddened quarrel, self-removal, curse pretext, Prabhasa) all match BP 3.3.13-14 and the pack's canonical cross-ref. Only the framing as a spoken dialogue with Uddhava is dramatised recall. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: After the Yadavas perished at Prabhasa, Krishna set the aftermath in motion: he sent Daruka to the Kurus to summon Arjuna and dispatched Vabhru to guard the women, then entered Dwaraka, touched his father's feet, and asked him to protect the ladies until Arjuna/Dhananjaya came.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4 (in pack): 'Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus...'; 'Do thou go quickly for protecting the ladies...'; 'Entering the city of Dwaravati, Janardana said these words unto his father, Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes'; 'Krishna touched the feet of his father with his head.' (Errand order is compressed; MB 16.4 has them find Rama first, then send Daruka/Vabhru, then visit the city, then return to find the serpent issuing.)

statements.claim: Krishna found Balarama sitting in a solitary spot with his back against a tree, absorbed in Yoga.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Keshava beheld Rama sitting in a solitary spot thereof. He also saw that Rama had set himself to Yoga'; 'reclining his back against a tree, in a solitary spot of earth.'

statements.claim: A great serpent issued from Balarama's mouth: white as snow, huge as a mountain, crowned with a thousand hoods, red-eyed — Sesha, leaving the human body it had dwelt in.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'from out his mouth was issuing a mighty snake. The colour of that snake was white. Leaving the human body (in which he had dwelt so long), that high-souled naga of a 1,000 heads and having a form as large as that of a mountain, endued besides with red eyes, proceeded along that way which led to the ocean.' VP 5.37 (pack index): 'The great serpent Śesha issues from the mouth of Ráma.'

statements.claim: The ocean came forth to receive Sesha, with the kings of the serpents (Karkotaka, Vasuki, Takshaka, Prithusravas, Sankha, Kumuda, Pundarika, Dhritarashtra, Hrada, Kratha, Sitikantha, Chakramanda, Atishanda, Durmukha, Amvarisha), the sacred rivers and Varuna at their head.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Ocean himself, and many celestial snakes, and many sacred Rivers were there... There were Karkotaka and Vasuki and Takshaka and Prithusravas and Varuna and Kunjara, and Misri and Sankha and Kumuda and Pundarika, and the high-souled Dhritarashtra, and Hrada and Kratha and Sitikantha... and Chakramanda and Atishanda, and that foremost of Nagas called Durmukha, and Amvarisha, and king Varuna himself.' (Story omits Kunjara and Misri — abridgement, not error.)

statements.claim: They offered Arghya and water for his feet, performed the rites of honour and saluted him with the customary enquiries; saints and serpents hymned him as the white form passed into the deep.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'offering him the Arghya and water to wash his feet, and with diverse other rites, they all worshipped the mighty Naga and saluted him by making the usual enquiries'; VP: the snake 'entered into the waters of the deep'; pack index summary: 'enters the ocean, hymned by saints and serpents.'

statements.claim: Krishna watched, then wandered thoughtfully in the forest, recollecting Gandhari's words, the brahmin's imprecation, the iron bolt, the quarrel at Prabhasa, and Durvasas' words over the remnant of the payasa he had eaten as Krishna's guest.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'he had thought before this of everything that had been fore-shadowed by the words uttered by Gandhari in former days. He also recollected the words that Durvasas had spoken at the time his body was smeared by that Rishi with the remnant of the Payasa he had eaten (while a guest at Krishna's house).' The curse/bolt/quarrel items are the same recollection (MB 16.4: 'thinking of the destruction of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas').

statements.claim: Krishna then sat down on the bare earth, the forest keeping watch — Balarama's remaining body like a tree with its spirit departed.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4 confirms Krishna 'sat down on the bare earth' after wandering thoughtfully; the tree-with-spirit-departed simile and 'forest kept watch' are atmospheric framing of the departure scene.

notes: Very close to MB 16.4 (Ganguli), with the full serpent-name catalogue and honours scene intact; VP 5.37 supplies the naming of Sesha. The single structural liberty is compressing the errands (Daruka/Vabhru/Dwaraka visit) into one continuous pre-forest sequence — MB has Krishna find Rama first, do the errands, then return to see the serpent — an ordering compression, not a contradiction. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Dreadful omens rose in Dwaraka — birds wheeling in unfamiliar circles, the sea holding its breath — and the city felt something coming.
statements.evidence: BP 11.30 has Krishna call the portents 'dreadful omens... the banners of death' (pack excerpt); the specific imagery (birds' circles, the sea's stillness) is atmospheric expansion of 'the omens reached Dwaraka,' not pack text.

statements.claim: Krishna told the Yadava elders: 'These dreadful omens are the banners of death. Not for a moment should we remain here. Let the women, the children, and the old ones go to Shankhoddhara. We will go to Prabhasa, where the Sarasvati flows westward, and worship there.'
statements.evidence: BP 11.30.4-9 (pack excerpt): 'These dreadful omens are the banners of death; not for a moment should we remain here. Let the women, children and elders go to Shankhoddhara, and let us go to Prabhasa where the Sarasvati flows westward.' Elders answered 'so be it' (iti sarve samākarṇya yadu-vṛddhāḥ, v.9).

statements.claim: The elders of the Yadus answered 'So be it' and the great departure began; the women, children and old turned toward Shankhoddhara at the parting of the ways while the rest pressed on to the mouth of the Sarasvati.
statements.evidence: BP 11.30.5 and 9: women/children/elders to Śaṅkhoddhāra; the Yadu elders assent. BP 3.3.24: after some months the Vrishnis, Bhojas and Andhakas went to Prabhasa; crossing to the mainland from the island city is the canonical setting of the tirtha journey.

statements.claim: Krishna linked the omens to Gandhari's curse: at the close of the great war the bereaved queen had cried out against him, promising ruin to his race as ruin had come to hers.
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt) confirms the operative frame: Krishna 'endeavoured to bring about those occurrences which would make Gandhari's words true.' The one-line gloss of what Gandhari had said at the war's end summarises that earlier curse scene (canonical in the corpus chain) rather than restating this pack's text.

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'The fourteenth lunation has been made the fifteenth by Rahu once more... It has once more appeared, it seems, for our destruction.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt): 'The fourteenth lunation has been made the fifteenth by Rahu once more... It has once more appeared, it seems, for our destruction.'

statements.claim: The Mahabharata says plainly that Krishna moved to bring about what Gandhari's words foretold, commanding the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to a sacred water.
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt): 'Vasudeva, having said so, endeavoured to bring about those occurrences which would make Gandhari's words true. That chastiser of foes commanded the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to some sacred water.'

statements.claim: Months passed before the great gathering assembled; the camp spread along the western shore with boats beached in rows and smoke of ten thousand cooking fires.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.24: 'after some months' the clans went joyfully to Prabhasa (katipayair māsaiḥ). The scale of the camp and cooking-fire imagery is descriptive colour consistent with a multi-clan assembly at the shore; the beached boats follow from the sea crossing.

statements.claim: Uddhava remembered that they went joyfully, deluded by fate: they bathed in the sacred waters, honoured the gods and rishis, and gave the brahmins cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants and lands.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.24-27 (pack excerpt and Sanskrit): 'saṃhṛṣṭā rathair deva-vimohitāḥ' — joyful, deluded by fate; v.25-26: they bathed, honoured the gods and rishis and gave cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants (ibhān), maidens and land. Pack excerpt: 'gave the brahmins cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants and lands.'

statements.claim: Krishna went with them, bathed and gave with them, letting them have their last happy days at Prabhasa since the curse would ripen wherever they stood.
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing of Krishna's known foreknowledge and acceptance (BP 3.3.13-14 deliberation, MB 16.2 'endeavoured to bring about...'); the emotional reading of the final good days is the story's commentary, not a pack statement.

notes: Two source strands are combined cleanly (BP 11.30.4-10 for the command/Shankhoddhara split; BP 3.3.24-27 for the joyful, fate-deluded journey and gifts; MB 16.2 for Rahu and Gandhari's words). Krishna's speeches are near-verbatim. Omens imagery and the Gandhari backstory gloss are connective; the Gandhari curse scene itself is the referenced antecedent (MB 16.2 'make Gandhari's words true'). No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: One day the sages Vishvamitra, Kanwa and Narada arrived in Dwaraka, and Vrishni heroes, Samva among them, decided to sport with them — already afflicted by the deities' rod of chastisement.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'the Vrishni heroes numbering Samva amongst them, saw Vishvamitra and Kanwa and Narada arrived at Dwaraka. Afflicted by the rod of chastisement wielded by the deities, those heroes, causing Samva to be disguised like a woman, approached those ascetics.'

statements.claim: They presented the disguised Samva (heir of Vasudeva) as the wife of Vabhru, desirous of a son, and asked what she would bring forth.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'This one is the wife of Vabhru of immeasurable energy who is desirous of having a son. Ye Rishis, do you know for certain what this one will bring forth?'

statements.claim: The rishis, eyes red with wrath, answered that Samva, heir of Vasudeva, would bring forth a fierce iron bolt for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas; the wicked, pride-intoxicated boys would through it become the exterminators of their own race, with the exception of Rama and Janardana.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'with eyes red in wrath... This heir of Vasudeva, by name Samva, will bring forth a fierce iron bolt for the destruction of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas. Ye wicked and cruel ones, intoxicated with pride, through that iron bolt ye will become the exterminators of your race with the exception of Rama and Janarddana.'

statements.claim: The sages added that the plough-armed hero would cast off his body and enter the ocean, and a hunter named Jara would pierce the high-souled Krishna as he lay on the ground.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'The blessed hero armed with the plough will enter the ocean, casting off his body, while a hunter of the name of Jara will pierce the high-souled Krishna while lying on the ground.'

statements.claim: The three sages then went to see Keshava; Krishna heard them, summoned all the Vrishnis, told them of it, said 'That which is destined will surely happen', and entered his mansion, not wishing to ordain otherwise.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'Having said so they then proceeded to see Keshava. The slayer of Madhu, informed of what had taken place, summoned all the Vrishnis and told them of it... he simply said that that which was destined would surely happen. Hrishikesa having said so, entered his mansion. The Lord of the universe did not wish to ordain otherwise.'

statements.claim: The next day Samva brought forth the iron bolt, fierce and like a gigantic messenger of death; through it all the individuals of the Vrishni and Andhaka races were to be consumed into ashes. The fact was reported to the king.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'When the next day came, Samva actually brought forth an iron bolt through which all the individuals in the race of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas became consumed into ashes... a fierce iron bolt that looked like a gigantic messenger of death. The fact was duly reported to the king.'

statements.claim: Ugrasena, in great distress, had the bolt ground to fine powder and men cast the powder into the sea.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'In great distress of mind, the king (Ugrasena) caused that iron bolt to be reduced into fine powder. Men were employed, O king, to cast that powder into the sea.'

statements.claim: At the command of Ugrasena (Ahuka), Krishna, Rama and the high-souled Vabhru it was proclaimed that no Vrishni or Andhaka might manufacture wine or intoxicating spirits, on pain of being impaled alive with all his kinsmen; through fear of the king and of Rama's word the people obeyed.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'At the command of Ahuka, of Janarddana, of Rama, and of the high-souled Vabhru, it was, again, proclaimed throughout the city that from that day, among all the Vrishnis and the Andhakas no one should manufacture wines and intoxicating spirits of any kind, and that whoever would secretly manufacture wines and spirits should be impaled alive with all his kinsmen. Through fear of the king, and knowing that it was the command of Rama also of unimpeachable [authority]... the people obeyed.'

statements.claim: Closing gloss: the powder had only been hidden, not recalled — 'the words of rishis, once spoken, do not dissolve in salt water' — and Dwaraka went dry overnight while the curse kept its own time.
statements.evidence: The ban and the sea-casting are pack-supported; the sea-keeping-its-secret reflection and 'emptied their jars' imagery are the story's ominous commentary on the unspent curse, not pack assertions.

notes: Nearly verbatim MB 16.1 (Ganguli): disguise, triple curse, sages' visit to Keshava, Krishna's 'destined' acceptance, next-day bolt, Ugrasena's grinding, and the wine prohibition with its impalement penalty all track the passage exactly. The 'sat down at the city's edge' and closing reflections are connective. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: After the slaughter at Prabhasa, Krishna walked out with his charioteer Daruka and Vabhru, following in the wake of Rama to discover his retreat; they found him sitting thoughtfully in a solitary spot, his back against a tree.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Then Daruka and Keshava and Vabhru left that spot, following in the wake of Rama (for discovering his retreat). They beheld that hero of infinite energy sitting thoughtfully, reclining his back against a tree, in a solitary spot of earth.' (Folded arms and 'strength gone out of him' are descriptive colour.)

statements.claim: Krishna commanded Daruka: 'Go to the Kurus. Inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly, hearing of the destruction of the Yadavas through the brahmin's curse.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly, hearing of the destruction of the Yadavas through the Brahmana's curse.'

statements.claim: Daruka, deprived of his senses by grief, climbed onto his car and drove toward Hastinapura, the capital of the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Thus addressed, Daruka, deprived of his senses by grief, proceeded on a car to the (capital of the) Kurus.' Hastinapura is the Kuru capital named throughout the MB's framing of this errand; 'climbed onto his car' is faithful rendering.

statements.claim: Krishna commanded Vabhru to go quickly and protect the ladies, letting no robbers injure them, tempted by the wealth with them.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Do thou go quickly for protecting the ladies. Let not robbers do them any injury, tempted by the wealth (that is with them).'

statements.claim: Vabhru — still helpless with wine but cheerless at the slaughter of his kinsmen — departed; once he had gone a little distance, the iron bolt attached itself to a mallet in a hunter's hands and sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him, for he too was named in the brahmins' curse.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Vabhru, still helpless with wine but cheerless at the slaughter of his kinsmen, departed. He had rested for a while by the side of Keshava, but as soon as he had proceeded to a distance, the iron-bolt, attaching itself to a mallet in the hands of a hunter, suddenly sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him, who also had been included in the curse of the Brahmanas.'

statements.claim: Krishna beheld Vabhru's death and did not move; he told Balarama: 'Wait for me here till I place the ladies under the care of kinsmen.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Beholding Vabhru slain, Keshava of great energy addressed his elder brother and said, Do thou, O Rama wait for me here till I place the ladies under the care of kinsmen.'

statements.claim: Entering Dwaravati, Krishna told his father to protect all the ladies of the house till Dhananjaya came, saying he would meet Rama that day, that he had beheld this carnage as he had beheld the Kuru carnage, that he could not see the city without the Yadavas, and that he would practise penances in the woods with Rama.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Janardana said these words unto his father, Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes. At the skirts of the forest Rama is waiting for me. I shall meet him today. This great carnage of the Yadus has been beheld by me even as I beheld before the carnage of those Kshatriyas who were the foremost ones of Kuru's race. It is impossible for me to see this city of the Yadavas without the Yadus beside me. Know that proceeding to the woods I shall practise penances with Rama in my company.' Krishna then 'touched the feet of his father with his head, and quickly left his presence.'

statements.claim: The ladies and children wailed; Krishna retraced his steps and said: 'Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.' Then he walked out of Dwaraka toward the forest.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Then a loud wail of sorrow arose from the ladies and children of his house... Keshava retraced his foot-steps and said unto them, Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.' The closing image of the yellow robe against the trees anticipates Jara's sight of the man 'dressed in yellow robes' (same chapter, in pack).

notes: Verbatim-faithful MB 16.4 (Ganguli): Daruka's errand, Vabhru's command and iron-bolt death, Krishna's speech to his father, the wailing and the consolation all match the passage sentence-for-sentence. Minor descriptive colour (folded arms, robe growing small) is connective. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Arjuna returned from Dwaraka to Hastinapura broken and weeping — face withered with grief — and wiped his eyes with his hand as he stood before Yudhishthira.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.1-2 (Sanskrit): 'śokena śuṣyadvadana' (face withered by grief), 'pāṇinā... āmṛjya netrayoḥ' (wiping his eyes with his hand); pack index: 'Arjuna returns from Dwaraka broken and weeping and tells Yudhishthira.'

statements.claim: He remembered the friendship, affection and intimacy of the years when Krishna was his charioteer — at Draupadi's svayamvara when the kings burned with envy, and at the burning of Khandava when he fought the gods themselves.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.3, 6-7: 'sakhyaṃ maitrīṃ sauhṛdaṃ ca sārathyādiṣu saṃsmaran' (recalling friendship, affection and the charioteering); v.6 the svayamvara at Drupada's house before kings maddened with desire; v.7 'aham u khāṇḍavam agnaye 'dām indraṃ ca sāmaragaṇaṃ tarasā vijitya' (I gave Khandava to Agni, conquering Indra with his hosts).

statements.claim: He remembered the sage Durvasa whose terrible hunger had once threatened the Pandava house, and how Krishna had come to them in the forest and turned the danger aside.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.10: 'yo no jugopa vana etya durantakṛcchrād durvāsaso' — Krishna protected them in the forest from the great calamity of Durvasa.

statements.claim: He remembered the Gandiva bow and every campaign it had won at Krishna's side, and Krishna's voice calling across the chariot — 'O Partha, O Arjuna, my friend, son of Kuru's race'.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.11-12 (Gandiva and its victories, won with Krishna) and v.17: 'narmāṇy... he pārtha he 'rjuna sakhe kurunandana' — the jests, 'O Partha, O Arjuna, friend, son of Kuru'; v.18 the shared laughter at play.

statements.claim: He told the king that the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drank the varuni, the madira wine, until their minds were churned and they were beside themselves, and in that madness slew one another with their bare fists, brother against brother, until the seashore of Prabhasa ran with their blood; of the whole race only four or five were left.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.21-22 and pack excerpt: 'In the city of our friends, the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drinking the madira wine and beside themselves, slew one another with their bare fists; but four or five were left.' Sanskrit v.22: 'vāruṇīṃ madirāṃ pītvā madonmathitacetasām' (drinking varuni/madira, minds churned). Prabhasa as the location of the fratricide is the same Uddhava recollection's setting (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain (DKS_0523 'The Yadava Fratricide at Prabhasa').

statements.claim: Krishna had taken up that body the way an actor takes up a costume and cast it off when the earth's burden was lightened — leaving the world at his own hour.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.33-34: 'yayāharad bhuvo bhāraṃ tāṃ tanuṃ vijahāv ajaḥ / yathā matsyādirūpāṇi dhatte jahyād yathā naṭaḥ' — the Unborn cast off the body that had borne the earth's burden, as an actor (naṭaḥ) takes up and drops forms like the fish-avatars. The 'own hour' framing reflects the same departure by the Lord's will.

statements.claim: In the very moment Mukunda abandoned the earth, the Kali age entered — the age of quarrel, the cause of all evil for the unawakened.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.35 and pack excerpt: 'when Mukunda abandoned this earth, in that very moment the Kali age, the cause of all evil for the unawakened, entered.'

statements.claim: Kunti too heard of the destruction of the Yadavas and the Lord's going, and took the measure of it in silence.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.31-32: 'pṛthāpy anuśrutya dhanañjayoditaṃ nāśaṃ yadūnāṃ bhagavadgatiṃ ca tām' — Pritha (Kunti) also heard, from Arjuna's words, of the destruction of the Yadavas and of the Lord's going. Her silent reckoning is connective rendering of her listening.

statements.claim: Closing scene: the sun rose over Hastinapura as always, the walls stood and the river ran, and only the wise could feel that the age itself had changed.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric epilogue to the Kali-age entry; the ordinary-day imagery is the story's closing reflection, not pack text.

notes: Faithful to BP 1.15 (Arjuna's grief and recollections, the varuni-madira fratricide report, 'four or five left', the actor simile, Kali age at Mukunda's departure, Kunti's hearing). Every memory (svayamvara, Khandava, Durvasa, Gandiva, Krishna's call) maps to a specific verse of the chapter. Prabhasa in the slaughter sentence is the canonical location from the same Uddhava account (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.
